t: October 14th, 752 p.m.
You're in your grandfather's barn,
fixing the fan on an airpipe nobody has used since 1962.
Your phone screams.
Then the sky to the west turns white.
No sound.
Not yet.
60 miles away, Omaha is gone,
and you have maybe an hour before the fallout gets here.
You're going to spend the next 10 years under this barn.
For the first five,
staying down there is the smartest thing you'll ever do.
For the last five, it's the biggest mistake of your life.
And you won't know which is which until you open the hatch.
The barn is lit like noon.
Every nail throws a black shadow.
Then the light goes orange and fades.
Sound travels about a mile every five seconds.
60 miles, five minutes before it gets here.
You start counting without meaning to.
The yard light dies.
So does every light on the county road.
The radio in your truck is still talking.
A man reading too fast.
This is not a test.
Then three words from posters nobody ever read.
Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.
Cows bellowing in the north pasture.
A pickup flying past with its horn held down.
A second flash farther north.
You throw firewood off the pile.
Underneath, set into the floor, is a square of steel.
You haul it open.
Three minutes.
Four.
At five, it arrives.
Not a bang, a long rumble.
Like a freight train passing under the whole county.
The farmhouse windows buzz.
Dust rains from the rafters.
Under your hand, the steel lid hums.
12 feet of ladder.
Hatch shut.
Wheel spun until it stops.
At the bottom, around a corner, a second door.
You close that too.
In the dark, the radio in your bag says it one more time.
Stay tuned.
And then there's only hiss.
In 1961, President Kennedy told American families
to build fallout shelters.
Most people laughed.
Your grandfather poured concrete.
In October 1962, during the Cuban Missile Crisis,
he spent three days down here.
The last entry in his log book?
Three days.
Came up.
World's still here.
He died three years ago and left you the farm.
Then the news went bad.
A little worse every month.
Pharmacies selling out of iodine pills,
the way they really did in 2022.
You spent every dollar you had rebuilding his shelter.
Tonight's fan was the last job.
Two concrete rooms.
One to live in, four bunks, a table, a stationary bike.
One for storage.
Here's how they keep you alive.
Every three and a half inches of packed dirt
cuts radiation in half.
Over your head, there are five feet of it.
About 100,000 times less.
And the inner door sits around a corner
because radiation mostly flies in straight lines.
Air comes in through a pipe hidden in a fence post,
bent downward so falling dust can't drop in.
A course filter, then a HEPA filter,
the kind hospitals use, catch the rest.
The fan pushes air in harder than it can leak out
so dust can't sneak through the cracks.
Old air leaves through a dead stump.
Close both valves and one person has about half a day
before the air starts to hurt.
10 years of bottled water would weigh 14 tons.
So you drink from a well.
Fallout is dust lying on the surface.
The water underneath is filtered
by every foot of dirt above it.
Sealed cap, hand pump.
No electricity needed to drink.
A solar panel on the barn roof and that bike.
Both charging one bank of batteries.
An hour of hard pedaling makes about 100 watt hours.
Enough for an LED bulb all day
or the fan for about three hours.
Food.
Two and a half years of groceries.
Oldest cans first.
Then the wall.
200 buckets of wheat and corn.
About three tons.
Sealed in foil bags with oxygen absorbers.
No oxygen means no bugs and no rot.
Packed like that, wheat lasts 30 years.
One bucket feeds one person for about 25 days.
Plus mushroom spawn, a tub of mealworms,
a radiation meter, iodine pills,
three courses of antibiotics,
and a box of spare filters.
Under your grandfather's last entry,
you write three rules.
One, nothing shows up top.
Two, nobody comes in.
Three, every voice is a stranger.
The first night, you learn about heat.
There isn't any.
12 feet down, the earth holds the bunker
near 50 degrees all year.
Never freezing, never warm.
You sleep in your coat.
The only flame is one propane burner.
Under a hood, vented into the exhaust
with a carbon monoxide alarm beside it.
20 minutes of cooking a day burns about
a gallon of propane a month.
The farm's buried tank holds hundreds.
And the toilet.
The barn sits on a slope,
so a pipe runs downhill to an old septic tank
buried lower than your floor.
Gravity does the work.
A bucket of well water flushes it
and a one-way valve makes sure nothing ever comes back.
For two weeks, you barely touch the fan.
Fallout fades fast.
Every time the hours since the blast multiply by seven,
the radiation drops by 10.
Seven hours, one tenth.
Two days, one hundredth.
Two weeks, about one thousandth.
You swallow an iodine pill,
so your thyroid is already full
when the radioactive kind arrives.
Then, you wait.
On day 15, the meter clicks slowly in the living room.
Next to the filter box, it clicks fast.
Your filter caught all that dust.
Now, it's the most radioactive thing you own.
You change it in gloves and a mask
and bury the old one in a sealed drum in the far corner.
The radio lasts seven weeks.
Lists of shelters.
Closed roads.
Then, a recording.
Then, nothing.
Without the sun, days start to slide.
In 1962, the same year your grandfather sat down here,
a French scientist named Michel Sifre
spent two months in a cave with no clock.
When his team called him up,
he was sure he still had a month to go.
So every morning, you make one mark in the logbook.
There was a camera on the barn roof.
Ash and Frost killed it the first month.
All you have now are your ears.
And up top isn't quiet.
Footsteps running across the field at night.
Someone screaming a name.
Someone crying in the barn, right over your head,
for an hour until they stop.
Gunshots, three or four a night.
Then, fewer.
You don't go up.
Rule one, July doesn't come.
The air from the intake is cold.
There's frost inside the pipe in the morning.
When it rains, it hisses like sleet.
Scientists who model nuclear war predicted this.
Smoke from burning cities climbs above the weather
and dims the sun for years.
Summers in the Midwest get too short for crops to ripen.
The solar panel is nearly dead.
The sky is the color of a dirty nickel.
So the bike does everything.
Astronauts on the space station work out two hours a day
to keep their bones from thinning.
Your gym makes electricity.
One hour of pedaling buys you three hours of breathing.
That winter, you make a mistake you can't see.
The air leaving the stump is 50 degrees
and wet with your breath.
Outside, it's 10 below.
It rises as a thin white plume.
And the warm pipe melts a perfect dark circle in the snow.
A white field, one stump, one steaming circle.
In the morning, you hear boots on the crust.
They walk around the stump once, twice.
Then they head for the barn.
That night, someone knocks on the hatch.
In year three, a voice will come down your air pipe.
You'll let it in.
A year later, you'll find out who sent it.
In March of year two, you spit in the sink and it's pink.
Your gums are bleeding.
A scrape on your knuckle won't close.
Scurvy.
Vitamin tablets lose strength over time
and dry grain has almost no vitamin C.
But soak a handful of wheat and keep it damp for two days
and as it sprouts, the seed starts making vitamin C
on its own.
A cup of sprouts a day and in three weeks,
your gums stop bleeding.
Then, tiny holes in a bag of rice.
Weevils.
Droppings in the oats.
A mouse came down the exhaust pipe.
You lose 40 pounds of food.
Everything unsealed goes into buckets
and the pipe gets a wire screen.
The mouse gets a name.
Then, a trap.
In August, something rattles down that pipe
and lands on the screen.
A page torn from a phone book wrapped around a rock.
We know you're down there.
Share and nobody gets hurt.
You read it four times.
You don't answer.
Rule three, two years.
You've started talking to the photo
of your grandfather on the shelf.
Great listener, terrible advice.
In April of year three,
you scrape out the last can of chili.
From now on, it's wheat.
Boiled wheat.
Sprouted wheat.
On Sundays, wheat with honey.
For the next seven years.
In September, a voice comes down the air pipe.
Hey, I can hear your fan.
Please, young, shaking.
You stand under the pipe and say nothing.
The second night, he's back.
His name is Cole.
He's 18.
He tore his leg open on a barbed wire fence.
Nobody has spoken to you in almost a thousand days.
You hear yourself answer.
The third night, you talk for an hour.
He tells you about his dad who knocked on his bedroom door
the same way every single morning.
You laugh for the first time in a year.
The fourth night, his voice is slurred.
The leg is hot.
Would you open the hatch?
Yes or no?
Tell me in the comments
before you find out what you did.
Because if you don't, you'll sit here
and listen to a man die at the end of your pipe.
You did that once already.
The first winter in the barn.
You can't do it twice.
So you open the hatch on your terms.
He comes down the ladder alone,
hands empty and strips to his underwear in the shaft.
The inner door stays shut
until you've seen every inch of that leg.
Rule two is gone.
The leg is infected.
You have three courses of antibiotics.
You give him one.
It's the most expensive thing you've ever handed anyone.
He sleeps for two days.
You don't.
The key to the inner door hangs on a string
around your neck
and the food log sleeps under your pillow.
How did you find me?
The steam, he says.
Everybody knows about the steam.
One upside, a resting person gives off
about as much heat as a 100 watt bulb.
The bunker is two degrees warmer.
You'll take it.
One morning, he taps five knocks on the bunk frame.
The rhythm every American knows.
Shave and a haircut.
Your knuckles answer before you think.
Two bits.
My dad's knock, he says.
From then on, it's how every morning starts.
Two people empty a bucket every 12 days.
So the storage room becomes a farm with no sun.
No grow lights.
A pound of lettuce under LEDs
takes about a hundred hours of pedaling for 70 calories.
Instead, oyster mushrooms, which grow on straw in the dark

Cole looks at the worm tub and says, absolutely not.
A week later, he asks for seconds.
He takes over the bike.
An hour every morning, an hour every night.
So I'm a hamster now.
A hamster who breathes.
In April, you wake to water hitting the floor.

Someone up top is feeding snow melt into the stump.
The floor floods.
The batteries spark.
The bedding is soaked.
You close the exhaust valve and it stops.
They weren't trying to drown you.
They wanted you to come up.
Six nights later, the pipe smells like burning tires.
You close both valves.
Two people, one sealed room.
By morning, your head is pounding
and Cole can't finish a sentence.
Carbon dioxide, building with every breath.
At dawn, the smoke is gone
and you pedal until the air tastes like air again.
In June, a calm, friendly voice comes down the pipe.
County rescue, we have food and medicine.
You can open up now.
Rule three, you don't move.

That's Dutch, he whispers.

They sent me.
Dutch saw the steam years ago.

I was supposed to unlock the inner door the first week.

You gave me your medicine.

August of year five.
For the first time in five years,
the air from the intake is warm.
You notice it.
You don't think about what it means.
That night, a voice comes down the pipe.

Cole, open the door and you eat.

You can't breathe.

Up top, something heavy hits the barn floor.

You don't have the air.
Then, the barn catches.

The roof coming down.
Then, nothing.

The steel held.

Concrete holds water

The ring is split all the way around.

You and Cole break apart two spare bunks

Boards crossed and wedged against the ring,

You step back.
It held, you say.
It won't hold twice.

After the fire, nothing breaks all at once.
It wears out.
The batteries hold a little less every year,

A molar goes bad.
There's no dentist.
There's Cole and a pair of pliers.

There's gray in your beard now.

That's real.
